rows.q: Katz says there is no economy. A sceptical economist replies that markets obviously coordinate millions of decisions with no center at all. How would Katz answer, and where is his answer weakest?
rows.a:
Katz would not deny the economist's observation. He would deny what the observation proves. The claim is easier to defend than its slogan suggests, and its weak points are fairly specific.

## What "no economy" means

Katz is not saying nobody trades or that prices don't move. The coauthored essay on this theme says its aim is to show "the 'economy' as nothing more than an ideological representation of our more primary debt relationship with the center" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-2)). The "center" is whatever holds joint attention and protects the arrangement everyone is acting inside: ultimately a sovereign, an issuer of money, a court that will enforce a debt. So the compressed version is "There is no 'economy.' There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1)). Markets are one way that distribution gets delegated.

## How Katz would answer

**1. He concedes the coordination point and relocates it.** He accepts the Hayekian claim that no planner could gather the dispersed knowledge. It is "of course true, but also a non-sequitur and a distraction," because a general also has to leave subordinates room, and "there will therefore be 'markets' all along the line." In his words, "The argument for markets is really saying no more than that you can’t do a very good job if you’re being micromanaged at every point along the way" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-12)). He defines a market as "what people without direct authority for maintaining the social center do with knowledge, information and skills when they are being protected and bounded but not directly supervised by such authorities" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-1)). The words "protected and bounded" carry the argument: the decentralization is real, but it happens inside a perimeter someone maintains.

**2. Every market depends on a backstop.** He draws on Colin Drumm: a dealer quotes prices only because he bets that a larger "outside spread" will cover him if liquidity fails, so "something like a 'lender of last resort' is constitutive of any market" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-62)). Drumm's own phrase is that the market "is constituted by its anxiety about its own future existence" ([same](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-57)). Money is credit issued from the center, and the modern state is "a debt enforcement agency."

**3. Prices register power, not just scarcity.** Following Bichler and Nitzan, he holds that "it is power that makes the owned artefacts valuable to begin with" ([same](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-68)). A price is an expectation about who will be able to enforce what.

## Where the answer is weakest

**It slides between two senses of "center."** The center as joint attention (what any shared scene needs) is nearly trivially true. The center as an occupied seat of enforcement, such as a central bank or an intelligence service, is a substantive and contestable claim. The economist can grant the first and the backstop point in the second and still say that day-to-day allocation runs on dispersed price signals. Drumm's lender of last resort explains crises, not how steel gets to the car plant on Tuesday. Katz's own capillary concession leaves the economist almost everything she asked for.

**It risks being unfalsifiable.** Any decentralized coordination can be reread as delegation or as the center's unseen margin. If the capillaries count as "ritual distribution from the center," no observation could count against the thesis, which makes it a redescription more than a finding. Katz does say he wants his hypotheses "descriptive in a revealing way," so the fair test is whether the redescription predicts anything. It is strongest where the center's hand is visible (monetary policy, enforcement, regulatory capture) and thinnest on ordinary price formation.

**The historical argument doesn't settle the operational one.** That markets began as state provisioning for soldiers (Graeber, Seaford, as Katz uses them) is a point about origins. The economist will say origins don't determine how a mature market works.

**He has no worked-out replacement for prices.** This is where the economist presses hardest. Katz admits it: "I’m trying to imagine an advanced economy without prices and therefore without money, but also without central planning, and if that’s utopian, so be it" ([Can Networks Crowd Out Markets?](/post/can-networks-crowd-out-markets-gablog#p-5)). In [Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-18) he grants that "the only way of obtaining the needed information without prices is to close off the system, which is precisely what is deemed either impossible or terrifying." His proposed substitute, "controlled usurpations" across supply chains, is a sketch, not something tested.

The critique that does the most damage, then, is that "there is no economy" is a strong thesis about explanation backed by a weaker one about institutions, and the rhetoric leans on the strong one.

## Where to go next

- [Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog) is the clearest statement of his position on distributed knowledge, and it shows how much he concedes.
- [Monopoly](/post/monopoly) takes up the pricing problem directly. Read it as the place where he tries to meet your economist.

To test the thesis yourself, pick one price you can trace (a rent, a commodity) and ask, step by step, what the center is doing in that chain. Then ask whether the answer changes your prediction or only your vocabulary.

rows.q: I run a 40-person company and two senior people are fighting over who leads a new product. Use imperative exchange, the pointman and succession to tell me what to do on Monday.
rows.a:
I'll take it in Katz's terms first and then turn it into a Monday plan. The archive treats succession and imperative exchange at length. It never gives managerial advice, so the plan is my application, not his.

## The fight, read through the concepts

**Imperative exchange.** Katz's basic claim is that our relations to authority are exchanges of imperatives: "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)). When a rivalry like yours breaks out, one reading is that two people are each issuing a demand, "give me this product", and you are the only one who can answer with a command. Katz is blunt about the structure: "whatever your demand of the center, consider the kind of command that could limit and satisfy it better than it would itself know how to and then realize that your demand is really for such a command" ([Blockchaining the Center](/post/blockchaining-the-center#p-17)). Your two seniors are not really asking for the product. They are asking someone to settle who commands. If you stay silent, the demand escalates, because the exchange is left open and each of them has to improvise the missing command.

**The imperative gap.** There is always a gap between the command issued and the command obeyed. The dispute lives in that gap. Neither of them can know what you would decide, so each is building a case and gathering support. Katz says power is what closes this gap by making the chain of command legible, and that unclear succession is what keeps it open: "if you are not choosing your successor you are not actually in power, because everyone around you can hedge on various degrees of obedience and support by transferring promises of obedience and support to the more likely successors" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). Your two seniors are hedging, and each one's tacit question is whether the other will end up above them.

**The pointman.** This is Katz's recent word for the occupant of the center. The point of the role is to be the one the line of command runs through, and the test of whether you hold it is simple: "the pointman is determining credit." You are the pointman here. The fight is evidence that this is not yet fully clear to the two of them, or that it is clear and they are testing it.

**Succession.** Katz's claim is that continuity is the real issue under most disputes: "you want to select someone who will in turn select someone who will in turn select someone" ([same essay, p-3](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)). Applied to your case, the product lead is a position, and you should be asking who is best placed to lead it and also to pick and develop who comes after. He adds that the selection is never final: "The selection would not be made once and for all... the occupant will himself revise his expectations" ([p-8](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-8)). That means you can decide now and keep the decision revisable on stated terms.

## What this suggests for Monday

1. **Decide the question yourself and say so.** Katz is clear that the center cannot be a committee. The decision does not need to be popular, but its source needs to be unmistakable. Don't ask the two of them to work it out; that prolongs the open exchange.

2. **Give a command, not a compromise.** A split lead or a vague "collaborate" leaves the gap exactly where it is. Name one lead. If the second person gets something real, make it a different, named responsibility with its own scope, so it is not a consolation.

3. **Say what the decision is for.** Katz treats the command as one that "limits and satisfies" demand better than the demand itself could. So give the reasoning in terms of the product and the company's continuity, for example who is better placed to build a team that can run this without you. Avoid ranking the two as people.

4. **Make the succession logic visible.** Tell both of them what you are looking for in whoever leads, including their ability to develop a successor. Then the loser has a criterion to work toward instead of a grievance to carry.

5. **Hear the two of them separately first.** This is my suggestion, not Katz's, but it fits his scenic point that resentment looks for a hearing. Each should get one private conversation before the announcement, where you listen and then tell them what you will do. Katz's term for the final state is that they should be able to "donate" the resentment, meaning give it up to the center and get something back, and that is far likelier if they have been heard and the decision is firm.

6. **Set a review date.** Katz's succession is a continuing practice. Pick a date for revisiting the lead role on stated criteria. This keeps the loser's hope honest and keeps the winner accountable.

## Where Katz would push back

He would say your task is smaller than "pick the better person." The conflict reveals that your own succession arrangements, the question of who leads and who comes after, are not settled at the center. If this is the second dispute of its kind, the fix is to publish how leads get chosen, not to adjudicate each case.

I should also be clear about the limits. Katz writes about sovereignty, scenes and credit, not about running a 40-person company, and nothing in the archive tells you who in particular is right. The facts of the product, the two people and your own position matter a great deal, and you know them.

## To read next

- [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity). The shortest statement of why choosing your successor is what authority consists of.
- [Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession). Develops the pointman and how credit is conferred through succession and ranking.

A question to try on yourself before Monday: if you announced this decision and then left for a month, what would each of the two do, and what does that tell you about who has actually been treating you as the center?

rows.q: What exactly is idiomclining, how is it different from coining jargon, and can you idiomcline this sentence of mine: "Our team needs better communication"?
rows.a:
Idiomclining is Katz's name for a practice with language, and it is easier to see by contrast with what it replaces.

## What it is

The word is built from "cline," a gradual, imperceptible shift from one state to another. Katz notes that it survives in "incline" and "decline," and that "upcline" is "a way of 'resisting' the more passive 'incline' and catastrophic 'decline'" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16)). That "upcline" comes from an earlier essay on grammaticization, which isn't among the texts I have, so I can only report how Katz sums it up here. In grammaticization, a word drifts toward a purely grammatical function, and upclining pulls it back toward meaning.

The practice itself: "dedicating oneself to setting relatively immobilized 'pieces' of language back into motion seems a good way of thinking about operating within an idiom" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17)). Katz admits you will be mistaken in doing it, since you'll violate some expectation, but "you also can't go wrong because you present a opportunity for an adjusted response on the part of others." So it is a way of stopping to think as a form of doing, and he offers it in place of "critical thinking," which he calls a bureaucratized category.

His target is a class of words, "cognition," "consciousness," "belief," "communication," that name measures which then get turned into targets ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-1)). An idiom, for him, is a particular run of ostensive, imperative, interrogative and declarative moves around a center. Learning one means learning "when, for example, someone asking a question or making a statement is really requesting that you do something" ([Scenic/Event Intelligence](/post/scenic-event-intelligence#p-13)).

## How it differs from coining jargon

Both can produce words only insiders understand, but they point in opposite directions.

Jargon, in Becker-Ho's account as Katz reviews it, "defends and reinforces a world based on the division of labor by protecting the privileges of a caste" ([Book Review: The Essence of Jargon](/post/double-helix-v4-becker-ho-review#p-10)). It marks distance and membership. Katz also warns that "nominalization can freeze discourse into jargon," and that the remedy is to use nominalizations to generate more verbal activity ([Technology and Magic, Doings and Happenings](/post/technology-and-magic-doings-and-happenings#p-21)). A new coinage that settles a dispute by being a coinage is the pattern he distrusts.

Idiomclining asks the opposite of a word: "make your idiom both more idiomatic and more transferable" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-15)). It should fit this exchange so closely that it speaks only to the person in it, and it should also be something either of you could carry to anyone else.

Katz does not oppose specialized vocabulary. He says he is always developing one for Center Study, "even if it impedes popularization," because "it enhances compressibility" ([Compression](/post/compression#p-9)). He also applies the warning to himself: idiomatic features "can become so formulaic as to mark belonging to a impenetrable bureaucratic space. There must always be space for idiom generation within the idiom" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-10)). A term like "idiomclining" is jargon the moment it stops being used to unfreeze something.

## Your sentence

What follows is my application, not Katz's, and he would say it will be wrong somewhere. It is still the kind of move he describes.

"Communication" is the frozen piece. It is a nominalization of verbs like say and know, and "better" is a measure with nothing to point at. Everyone can agree with the sentence and nothing changes. Katz makes the same complaint about "be clear": such terms have "a sense and referent for those practiced in assessing writing... but none at all for the person doing the thinking and writing" ([The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-13)). It is also a declarative that hides a demand. Someone wants something done, and the sentence doesn't say what, from whom, or how anyone would know.

So turn the noun back into verbs, in the loop Katz uses elsewhere: identify something, make a change, show the result. For example:

*"When someone on our team sees a problem, they say what they see; whoever owns that part says what they will do about it; and a week later we look at the same thing together and say whether it's the same."*

This version gives a person something to do and something to point at. It also forces a question the original dodged, which is who owns "that part." You might have been avoiding that question, and "communication" conveniently covered for it.

You could test your own version by asking whether a teammate could obey it tomorrow, and whether someone on another team could pick it up and use it. If it fails, take the mistake as feedback and re-cline it.

## Where to go next

Read [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) itself; it's short, and the section on safe and dangerous scenes shows the practice under pressure. Then [The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage) for why terms like "clarity" and "communication" can't issue usable instructions, and what Katz proposes in their place. As an exercise, take a sentence from your workplace that everyone nods at, such as "we need to be more strategic," and try the same unfreezing on it.

rows.q: Explain how the ostensive, imperative and declarative relate to Katz's account of money as debt to the center, for someone who knows Girard well but has never read Gans.
rows.a:
Gans is what makes the money account possible, so I'll begin with the Girard-to-Gans step and then show how the three speech forms carry Katz's account of debt.

## From Girard to Gans

You'll know Girard's picture: mimetic rivalry builds to a crisis, the group turns on a scapegoat, and the sacred is born from the killing. Gans's complaint against it, as Katz summarizes, is that "without language there is no way for the original event to become meaningful to the group" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-3)). Animals kill their own kind constantly and nothing changes. So Gans puts a sign at the origin, and then the killing is no longer needed. A group converges on a desirable object and breaks the animal pecking order, and one member's grasp gets aborted in the middle. It becomes a gesture that the others imitate. The sign is shared, and so is the center it points at.

Katz stresses that this first sign is "an ostensive sign—that is, it is inextricable from the event in which it is issued and therefore constitutes the object it refers to" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-6)). So the ostensive is pointing that also creates the thing pointed at: the sacred center. Gans's name for the gesture is the "gesture of aborted appropriation"; I'm supplying that from Gans, though Katz uses it throughout.

## The other two forms (plus a middle one)

For Gans, the imperative and the declarative are not inventions someone wanted. They arise as repairs of mistakes. Katz puts it this way: "the first imperative was an 'inappropriate ostensive'", someone names an object that isn't there and someone else fetches it ([Originary Mistakenness, Defilement and Modernity](/post/anthropoetics-originary-mistakenness#p-18)). The interrogative is a "prolonged, which is to say, botched imperative." The declarative comes when an imperative can't be fulfilled: it "has its origins in the 'negative ostensive,' the response to the 'inappropriate imperative,' where the object cannot be provided, the imperative cannot be fulfilled, and linguistic presence is therefore threatened" ([Cognition as Originary Memory](/post/cognition-as-originary-memory#p-11)).

Katz adds his own reading of this last step. The declarative's "don't" runs in two directions at once: it tells the person demanding to stop, and it relays an order from the center that the object be absent. He calls this a "bidirectional imperative," and reality is thereby constructed as something that refuses our demands ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-7)). A declarative is a command from the center that limits a demand.

## Where money enters

Now ask what these forms are for. Katz's answer is that they are not first of all tools for transmitting information. They are a way of keeping an exchange with the center going. He calls that exchange an "imperative exchange" and associates it with prayer. The center commands, we petition, and "an imperative, whether it be a command, demand or anything in between, always looks forward to some exchange" ([Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection: Expectant Scenes](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes#p-6)).

The object on the originary scene was given, in that it let itself be shared. So everyone who takes part owes something back. Katz's formulation: "I've scaled up deferral as originary debt, which is really unending gratitude toward the center, in whatever form the center might take" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-24)). Debt here is not first of all a financial notion. It is the standing relation that deferral creates between each of us and the center.

Money is then a late, scaled-up instrument of that relation. In the essay Katz wrote with Zack Baker, money is the center issuing receipts: "Money records, by the center, a debt paid to the center, and that record can in turn become a way of paying debts to the center" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-36)). Earlier in the same essay they quote Gans's own definition: money is "a credit drawn on the sacred that cannot be freely reproduced." Katz's shorthand is "Money is a bet on the future; more precisely, it is a partitioning and parceling out of the imperative of the center" ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-1)).

## How the three forms map onto debt

Here is how I would line them up, following Katz.

**Ostensive: the token and the receipt.** Money is something you can point at, and it only works if everyone sees the same thing there. Katz notes that an imperative isn't finished until compliance is itself witnessed, "kind of like the signature a delivery man requires or the photo the Amazon guy takes of your package at the door" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-8)). The ledger entry is that return ostensive.

**Imperative: the debt as obligation.** A loan or promise is a command that reaches into the future. It also depends on the continuity of the center, as Katz writes: "credit, moreover, is always a bet on succession, on the continuity of governance" ([Perfecting the Imperative and Imperative Exchange: Originary FinTech](/post/perfecting-the-imperative-and-imperative-exchange-originary-fintech#p-9)).

**Declarative: credit as projected, absent things.** The declarative creates a present in which absent things can be spoken of. "That's what the declarative does: generate new possible, hypothetical, potential ostensives, which also means new scenes upon which we might say 'this is the same'" ([Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes#p-9)). Credit works the same way: it speaks, in the present, about what will be shown later. Katz says it outright: "to speak in sentences is to draw upon and issue lines of credit. The debt we owe to the center is a product of deferral, and the lines of credit issued are therefore tokenized deferrals" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-9)).

A small example in Katz's own words: "If you lend me 100$ today I will pay you back in a year" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-11)). The sentence is a declarative resting on an imperative, with an ostensive checkpoint a year ahead. Whether it means anything depends on whether the governing and juridical institutions will look the same then. That is why Katz can call everyone's confidence in the dollar a bet on succession.

## Back to Girard

Katz does not treat debt as a harmless replacement for sacrifice. "Our language is permeated with sacrifice, ultimately, still, human sacrifice—some must die for the community to continue—because that has been the only social form of deferral we've ever had." His hope for money is that it can be converted so that "language will only be worth currency when we convert it sufficiently in ways that defer sacrifice" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-14); [#p-19](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-19)). In Girardian terms, debt is the ordered, ritualized form of what the scapegoat discharged violently, and its worst forms are the ones that go back to hostage-taking and ostracism.

To keep sources straight: the Girard and Gans specifics (the scapegoat mechanism, the "gesture of aborted appropriation") are background from outside the archive except where Katz restates them. The mapping of ostensive, imperative and declarative onto the structure of credit is Katz's own, built up across the recent essays rather than set out in one place, so my table above is a reading of those texts and not a single quotation.

## Where to go next

- [Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality) is the closest the archive comes to saying all this at once: language as credit and debt.
- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf) (with Zack Baker) is the long, academic version of the money argument, leaning heavily on Gans's essay on firstness.
- [Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes) shows how the grammar and the finance are woven together.

A small exercise: take any promise you've made recently and write out its three layers. What was being pointed at? What command did it carry into the future? And what declarative did you have to say in the present about something that wasn't there yet?

rows.q: Is singularized succession in perpetuity just monarchism? Give the strongest version of that objection and then Katz's reply.
rows.a:
## The strongest version of the objection

SSIP is monarchism with the crown filed off. Katz arrives at it by following absolutism through to its end: "the logic of concentrating actual power in nominal power," ending in the claim that "if you are not choosing your successor you are not actually in power" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). He calls it "the successor concept to 'absolutism'" ([Selving](/post/selving#p-21)), says "We are defenders of the Big Man revolution!" ([Threading through History](/post/threading-through-history#p-4)), and in the *Anthropomorphics* chapter on succession proposes that "the current occupant of the center chooses his successor." The objector adds three charges:

1. **Nothing outside the ruler checks it.** Whoever holds the center picks the next holder. That is cooptation, and it is exactly how a dynasty or a politburo reproduces itself.
2. **It is too formal to be tested.** If it fits a king, a CEO and a party boss alike, it excludes nothing.
3. **It rests on hope.** It assumes a good ruler. Katz concedes that "the successor such an occupant selects would not, in fact, succeed" under a bad one, but that is a prediction, not a safeguard.

## Katz's reply

**1. It is not a regime type, and it is not about hereditary kingship.** Katz says outright that he "considered it best to abstract away from the (one must admit) remote possibility of establishing hereditary monarchies across the world" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)). The concept "cuts against, without excluding, the most historically 'popular' means of monarchical succession, primogeniture, since succession is now understood as the outcome of competition and mentorship" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)).

**2. It deliberately outgrows the word "monarchy."** In [Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-2) he imagines a security firm's CEO assuming sovereignty and says "There would be no reason to assume that this process will establish the position of 'monarch.'" He treats the central figure as one pole of a continuum, with rapid hand-offs "like one might see in a baseball game a succession of relief pitchers, sometimes each one facing only one batter" ([p-4](/post/continuum-of-power#p-4)). What distinguishes it from monarchy is multiplication: "the multiplication of succession rituals would distinguish this order from monarchy, which has few and regularly set succession rituals (coronations)" ([p-3](/post/continuum-of-power#p-3)). "Monarchy remains a placeholder concept," useful mainly "in arguing with 'democrats' and 'republicans.'"

**3. It operates at every level, so it is not a claim about the throne.** The argument is that "viewing everyone, in every field of endeavor, as concentrating their efforts of selecting their successor, is the most powerful way of reading human practices" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)). Even liberal and left institutions "understand succession far better than the right side of liberalism, as they take great care in how power is packaged and handed over to the next generation of activists" ([Singularized Succession](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). So the claim is about what all institutions are already doing, not a preference for kings.

**4. The "formal" charge is accepted but turned around.** Katz grants the formula is formal, yet says it "provides a powerful principle of selection of one over another," and that it spans "a spectrum from ethnic orders... to more associative orders" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-10)). It is also meant as a diagnostic: "a flawed society is one in which succession is not attended to and accounted for and a pathological society is one in which succession is actually subverted" ([p-13](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-13)). So it ranks and criticises. Totalitarian leaders, he notes, never publicly name successors, and that counts as a symptom, not a pass.

**5. There are internal brakes, but they are not elections.**
- The designation is revocable and constantly revised, so it is "a marker of the occupant's purposes and assessment of the scene" ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-9)).
- Top candidates are kept from real power: "The way to prevent this is to prohibit the top-tier candidates from occupying positions in which they exercise any real power" ([Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-9)).
- The ruler is justiciable. In the rotating-dictator model the occupant "combines extreme concentration of power with simplicity of replacement," and can be sued, though he can countersue ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-15)).

**6. On the bad ruler, he bets on structure.** A weak occupant can't actually make a successor stick, because naming one "would be impossible... without upsetting the delicate balance of rivalries between the various agencies" that now live off the process ([Sufficiency](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-7)).

## Where the objection still bites

Points 1 and 3 do not fully answer the cooptation worry. The brakes in point 5 are designs Katz proposes, not things any existing order has. The reply to the "unfalsifiable" charge also depends on accepting his definition of power as the capacity to choose a successor. If you don't, the concept looks like absolutism with a larger vocabulary. His own framing invites that test: "the same assumptions that provide us with prescriptions also supply the descriptions" ([Staged Succession](/post/staged-succession-marginalizing-the-victimary-and-scapegoating-in-a-single-move#p-11)).

## What to read next

- [Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power): the clearest statement of why "monarchy" is only a placeholder.
- [Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship): the lawsuit and replacement mechanics, which give the best answer to the checks question.

A good exercise: pick an institution you know and try to say who its successor-selection really belongs to. Then ask whether that matches who actually holds power there.

rows.q: Trace how the concept of the center changes from Anthropomorphics to the recent essays on thirdness and data exchange. What stayed, and what was dropped?
rows.a:
The center stays as the thing everything gets traced back to. What changes is what Katz does with it: *Anthropomorphics* builds a theory of how human order is organized around a center, and the recent essays try to build working practices (cases, credit, data) for dealing with it. This is my reading of the texts, not a chronology Katz gives himself.

## What stayed

**The center comes before agency.** *Anthropomorphics* defines it as "Whatever can invoke and be referenced by an ostensive sign: the center is both cause and product of the sign—as cause it subsists beyond any particular reference, and as product it is continually renewed" ([The Centrality of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-centrality-of-the-center#p-1)). Agency follows from this: "It is the center, first of all, that has agency—human agency will later come to be modeled on the agency of the center" ([The Center and the Declarative](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-the-declarative#p-19)). The data essays keep the same structure with data in place of signs: "the center is whatever will turn out to have been furthest upstream of that" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-5)).

**Succession is where governance is tested.** The book's closing proposal is that "the current occupant of the center chooses his successor" ([Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-2)). Singularized succession in perpetuity is that proposal sharpened. He starts from "the most certain test that power was in fact held was that the sovereign selected his successor" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)) and adds the trans-generational demand that each successor select the next.

**Resentment is still routed to the center.** What changes is the form of the routing (see below).

## What changed

**1. From signifying/occupied center to a larger apparatus.** The book's central problem is a discrepancy: "Once the center has been humanly occupied, the problem becomes determining, or knowing, that the center as occupied is the same center as the center as signifying" ([Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center#p-19)). The later work doesn't drop this pair, but it adds a second distinction. In [Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-3) he returns to "the problem of the two centers": "the center as generative origin continued through the occupied social center, on the one hand, and the center as anything upon which joint attention is exercised." Under imperial conditions, he argues, the second kind of center draws our attention away from the social center and toward samples. [The Sample as Our Donation to the Center](/post/the-sample-as-our-donation-to-the-center#p-6) puts it as the originary object being "both the thing we attend to and the meta-person we obey," two features that "get separated as, over time, humans come to 'turn their back' on the center as issuer of imperatives."

**2. Money becomes debt and credit.** In the book money is a delegation from the center: "money is a form taken by the delegation of power, and is therefore a form of power itself" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-18)). Later the center becomes a creditor: "we're all indebted to the center—this is originary, not modern, but what is modern is that the value of our debt is determined by expectation of future earnings" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)). He also reads the English settlement as an event about the center: the state funded by the Bank of England together with "rotation in occupation of the center" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-1)).

**3. The juridical moves to the middle.** In the book, justice systems arrive as one development among others ("With money, markets and plural power centers comes justice systems," in the same paragraph of *Generativity*). Later it is "a kind of irreducible, if less originary, middle term between ritual (originary distribution) and the disciplinary" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-1)). Everything in the Thirdness project is framed around it.

**4. From critique to construction.** The book's critical weapon is the "super-sovereignty": liberalism's rights, consent and so on, standing in for the missing center. He still allows that concept ("I haven't used it much in a while but could easily pick it up at any time"), "even if I would now make the juridical... more central" ([The Problem of Obedience, Revisited](/post/the-problem-of-obedience-revisited#p-2)). The project now is to turn conflicts into cases and judgments into data exchange. Katz's pattern is that "Data exchange is always with the center" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-13)).

**5. Resentment.** In the book the moral posture is "donating your resentment to the center," a renunciation of rebellion "in the name of some super-sovereign" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-15)). Later that idiom "can now be given a more strictly economic meaning; i.e., it can be tokenized" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-1)). Katz also adds a new claim: "The center doesn't resent—that would serve as a definition of the center. But, of course, any occupant of the center will resent" ([same](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-15)). He now also doubts that resentment explains everything at scale, saying mimetic theory and GA fail at "whatever can't get reduced to the scale of a 19th century French novel" ([Muffled Transmission from the Center](/post/muffled-transmission-from-the-center-substack#p-17)).

**6. A new name for the occupant.** He derives "center" from "point" and writes, "I can now replace the clumsy 'occupant of the center' with 'pointman'" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-17)).

## What was dropped or demoted

The vocabulary of the sacred is the clearest case. In [Inscription](/post/inscription#p-3) he says "sacred," "religion" and "ritual" are not minimal enough, and that "We get much closer to minimality with a word like 'commemoration.'" The label "anthropomorphics" was set aside too, for the "more disciplinary sounding 'center study'" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)). I wouldn't call these repudiations. They are moves toward a thinner base vocabulary.

## Where to go next

- [Signifying Center, Occupied Center](/post/anthropomorphics-signifying-center-occupied-center): the book's version of the problem the later work inherits.
- [Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack): the clearest single bridge to the debt vocabulary.
- [Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness): the juridical and data exchange worked out in detail.

An exercise: take one sentence from [Learncoin](/post/learncoin) or [Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness) and find the *Anthropomorphics* sentence it is a translation of. You will usually find that it is a rewriting of the earlier claim.

rows.q: On Katz's account, why can a language model write fluent declaratives but not promise or deem? Does that argument hold up?
rows.a:
Katz doesn't put this as a claim about what language models lack. He puts it in terms of what a speech act is, and the short version is that the declarative is the one speech form that can be detached from whoever utters it.

## Why declaratives come easily

In Katz's grammar the declarative is the form most cut loose from its scene. It originates as a way of deferring a failed imperative ("not here, stop demanding it"), but once writing isolates it, it becomes the form we mistake for the whole of language. In the *Introduction to Disciplinarity* he says that "the ideal declarative sentence is one that could be uttered felicitously by anyone, anywhere, at any time" ([An Introduction to Disciplinarity](/post/introduction-to-disciplinarity#p-87)). A form whose ideal is speaker-independence is just what a system trained on written text should be good at. Fluent declaratives are cheap because the form is designed to carry no trace of who says it.

## Why not promise or deem

Promising and deeming sit in the ostensive-imperative-ostensive sphere, where who speaks, and under what authority, is the whole point. Katz writes that "deeming places us in the chain of originary debt to the center, and while we can readily understand why a human would deem something to be that thing in a way we would go along with, there's really no particularly good reason why we should accept deeming carried out by a computer program or algorithm" ([Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-13)). Just before that: "AIs can't 'deem,' or if they do deem, they have been authorized or deemed worthy to do so, by, ultimately, a human" ([same text](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-12)).

Promises work the same way. "A promise draws credit from the promisee and places one in debt" ([Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-10)). He adds that promising, indebting and issuing credit "are speech acts that cannot be reduced to computation, and are therefore the domain of decision," because "those broader conditions require humans to be reliable before they are predictable" ([same text](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-12)). A promise is a position in a ledger of enforcement and forgiveness, and someone has to be able to be held to it.

## Does it hold up?

The strongest part is the structural point. A promise has felicity conditions (standing, accountability, a debtor who can be enforced against or forgiven) that a fluent sentence doesn't automatically carry. That is a real asymmetry, and it doesn't depend on any claim about inner experience.

I think there are three weak points, and the first two are Katz's own.

1. **The empirical claim is flagged as unproven.** He proposes it "as a hypothesis that I as yet have no idea how to prove or disprove, or even whether proof is the relevant consideration," namely that when AIs simulate these acts "there will always be something 'off' that humans can detect, even if not describe" ([Toward a Curriculum…](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-14)). That is a detection claim, and detection claims erode as systems train against detectors. Katz knows this pattern: of the machine-human boundary he writes that the desire to insist on a distinction "merely inspires someone to try and automate that distinctly human feature" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-14)).

2. **"Being programmed negates those speech acts" sits oddly with his own anthropology.** He says we would see "that we weren't really doing it precisely because being programmed negates those speech acts" ([Toward a Curriculum…](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-17)). But elsewhere every human utterance is a citation, and "every utterance is to some extent a promise" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-12)). Humans are mimetically programmed all the way down in his picture, so programming alone cannot be what disqualifies the machine.

3. **His own escape clause may be the real answer.** If an AI deems when "authorized … by, ultimately, a human," then deeming by a delegate is how human institutions already work. A clerk or a court officer also deems under borrowed authority. On this reading, the machine's promise is no different in kind from a corporation's; what is missing is a creditor with standing and a debtor who can be held to account. That is a claim about institutions and credit, not about any essence of the human. I'd say it is the more defensible version of Katz's position, and also the less dramatic one.

So the argument holds as a point about where authority and debt reside, and is weaker as a claim that machines can never get it right.

## Where to go next

- [Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah) is where promising is set out as the most originary speech act, and where the claim about computation is made.
- [Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning) gives the counter-pressure: the human as that which keeps being re-specified once the previous specification is automated.

A question to take away: if deeming is a position in a chain of credit, what would it take for a machine to hold that position and be held to it, and would we then still want to say it only "simulates" deeming?

rows.q: Take the essays on Judaism as a civilizational blockchain. What is the argument, and how does it follow from the originary hypothesis?
rows.a:
The "essays" are really a short series. *Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain* is the capstone, and it leans on *A Cybernetics of Judaism*, *The Longest, Most Convoluted, Revised and Thickly Imagined Title Deed Possible*, and *The Political Infrastructure of Judaism*. I'll take the argument of the blockchain essay first, then trace how Katz gets there from the originary hypothesis.

## The argument

The essay opens with a claim about antisemitism's logic: "The existence of Jews is a scandal, and therefore their existence is an unmistakable sign of immeasurable and monstrous Jewish power." ([Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-1)) If the Jews are believed to control the courts, the media and the rest, then the existence of Jews is itself the proof, and no ordinary legal remedy can reach them. Hence the pull toward acting "extra-juridically," and the drift Katz sums up with a parenthesis: "The arc of antisemitism is long but bends towards accusing everyone else of being Jews." ([p-2](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-2))

He then argues that this belief is a fantasy, and that you can see it is one by asking for measurement: "If the Jews really control everything, there’s nothing you can do; if you can do something, they don’t really control everything but, rather, represent one of many power centers" ([p-3](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-3)). Ask the accuser to map the power and he will balk, because it would turn out to be partial and contestable.

His prescription is a vocation for Jews. A war against the Jews implies "a comprehensive vendetta," so Jews have a job suited to that: "maintaining all the institutional means of deferring vendetta." ([p-6](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-6)) He narrows what that means. He would "sharply curtail the leftist Jewish interpretation" of witnessing to injustice as being about "social injustices," confining it "strictly to the operation of the juridical within the terms of the nomos" ([p-9](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-9)). The core statement follows: "Jews should try to become a civilizational blockchain—recording social exchanges and disputes as objectively and permanently as we can." ([p-11](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-11))

The blockchain image is about records that cannot be quietly altered. Katz makes the same point elsewhere about writing: "Blockchain, then, must also be a kind of writing, and we want writing to approximate the qualities of blockchain." ([Tokenization](/post/tokenization#p-8))

## How it follows from the originary hypothesis

It follows through a chain of intermediate hypotheses, not by direct deduction.

1. **The center and the juridical.** From the originary scene Katz takes the center, and then the Big Man who occupies it. Under imperial conditions the juridical appears. He defines it as "placing a ceiling on the vendetta by introducing higher order arbitration" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-1)), and describes the imperial order as one that sets up "a justice system in which the right to revenge is disavowed on the condition that complaints will be heard and adjudicated in a “satisfactory” way" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-3)). The nomos is the originary distribution of land and authority that all later claims refer back to. Hence the essay's two tasks: keeping the vendetta below the juridical threshold, and keeping the nomos from being put on trial.

2. **Judaism's structural position.** Here Katz borrows a premise from Bernard Lamborelle: that the covenant began as a grant from an earthly lord. Judaism then becomes a revised title deed, and "Torah study is the ongoing work on the terms of the deed or bailment" ([Title Deed](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack#p-12)). The people serve empires, so "A nation of priests became a nation of scribes which means a nation of ledgerers" ([A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-6)). Judaism is "located in the imperative gap," between the command issued and the command obeyed ([Political Infrastructure](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-13)). A scribal people's natural contribution is keeping the record clear, which the blockchain essay states directly: "there’s no better preparation for being a civilizational blockchain" ([p-13](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-13)).

3. **Why the Jews draw the hostility.** Proximity to governance makes them a lightning rod. "Antisemitism" for Katz is "really about giving a name to hidden sources of power," and "the Jews serve as a meter measuring this gap" between power and legitimacy ([Political Infrastructure](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-3), [p-27](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-27)). The closing line of the blockchain essay has them recording the "penumbra" of attack on the juridical order itself.

## Things to hold onto

Katz flags the historical premise as hypothetical ([Political Infrastructure, p-10](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit#p-10)). The "normative Jew" claim (the observant Zionist in Israel) and the proposed duties are his own normative moves, which the originary hypothesis does not itself supply.

## Where to go next

- [A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism): the scribes-and-ledgers argument at full length, and the case for treating Jewish law as governance.
- [The Political Infrastructure of Judaism](/post/the-political-infrastructure-of-judaism-the-inscription-of-the-reality-and-vanit): the "reality and vanity of empire," which explains why the Jewish position oscillates.

As an exercise, try stating in your own words why a scribal people would be tied to the juridical rather than the priestly, and see whether that holds without the Lamborelle premise.
